ui.title: Radio Mode Identifier
ui.press: Press Listen: the signal scrolls here
ui.count: {n} signals, in the order of sheet 6
ui.mystTags: Listen and watch, then pick the right answer
ui.quizLead: Start listening, watch the spectrum, the waterfall and the footprint, then answer.
ui.f1: Signals simulated in the page (12,000 samples per second): those of sheet 6 of the OpenBookRadio book, other signals from the book, and bonuses. For radio signals (AM, FM, AIS, LoRa…), you see the simulated intermediate frequency, as on an SDR screen; some are scaled down or sped up, as stated. For AM, SSB, FM, FM stereo, ISS and fading, you hear the demodulated sound, as from the receiver's loudspeaker, while the screen shows the radio signal; the voice is a synthetic voice that says no real words.
ui.f2: Time runs downwards in the waterfall and the footprint. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license, free, not for sale.
ui.book_dl2: Download the OpenBookRadio book (free, PDF and EPUB, 13 languages)

am.h: The strength of the carrier follows the sound: the curve "swells" and "shrinks".
am.l: A fixed line in the centre (the carrier), with two identical sidebands on each side. About 6 to 9 kHz wide. Shortwave and medium-wave broadcasting, aviation (sheets 12 and 14).
r: A jingle, then the presenter over background music. The two sidebands are mirror images: you see the melody, then the voice, on each side of the carrier.

ssb.h: Only one sideband remains, without carrier: nothing when nobody speaks.
ssb.l: No central line, a single band about 2.7 kHz wide that only lives while someone talks. USB above 10 MHz, LSB below (radio amateurs). Badly tuned, the voice sounds like a "duck" (sheets 11 and 29).

fm.h: The amplitude stays fixed; the oscillations get closer or wider apart with the sound.
fm.l: The signal dances around its frequency, wider when the sound is loud: 12.5 kHz per channel in narrow FM (walkie-talkies, repeaters), 200 kHz for FM broadcasting (sheets 2 and 13).
r: At the end, the short "kshh": the squelch closes when the transmitter stops.

cw.h: The carrier is switched on and off: dashes and dots.
cw.l: A very thin line that breaks to the rhythm of Morse; a beep to the ear. Here "CQ" (sheet 48).
r: 20 words/min, 60 ms dot, at 700 Hz: "CQ CQ CQ DE F4ABC K"
Pure beeps, long and short, on a single note

rtty.h: The frequency jumps between two values, one for 0, one for 1.
rtty.l: Two parallel lines: 170 Hz apart for radio amateurs (45.45 baud), 450 or 850 Hz for weather bulletins. A steady "tidilidi" (sheet 32).
r: Baudot ITA2: 5 bits + start + 1.5 stop; mark 2125 Hz, space 2295 Hz

afsk.h: Two audio tones, 1200 and 2200 Hz, sent into an FM transmitter.
afsk.l: Seen after the FM receiver (loudspeaker sound): a band from 1200 to 2200 Hz, in short bursts. By ear, a one-second "grrrt" (sheets 35 and 36).
r: 0x7E flags then AX.25 data in NRZI

psk31.h: The frequency does not move, the phase reverses; the amplitude dips at each reversal.
psk31.l: A very thin line about 60 Hz wide, slightly "braided". Dozens of stations fit in 3 kHz (sheet 29).
r: Varicode: 0 = phase reversal, 1 = no change; when idle, two twin lines

ft8.h: The frequency goes up and down in steps of 6.25 Hz, 0.16 s per step.
ft8.l: Bands about 50 Hz wide lasting 12.6 s and coming back every 15 s, synchronised to the clock: several stations at once within 3 kHz, for example on 7.074 MHz (sheet 29).
r: 79 symbols of 0.16 s, three Costas patterns (start, middle, end); here eight stations

ft4.h: Four tones spaced 20.8 Hz, 20.8 baud: 105 symbols in 5 s, in 7.5 s time slots.
ft4.l: Bands about 90 Hz wide, shorter and wider than FT8, coming back every 7.5 s. 14,080, 7,047.5 kHz (sheet 29).

olivia.h: Eight tones spaced 31.25 Hz, one at a time, jumping at random; Walsh coding and interleaving.
olivia.l: A block of scattered dots over 250 Hz; decodes far below the noise. A small random melody to the ear (sheet 29).

hell.t: Feld Hell: writing with a carrier
hell.h: The carrier is switched on and off dot by dot: each letter is made of columns of 14 dots, scanned from bottom to top (245 dots per second).
hell.l: On the waterfall, a chopped line; the software screen (fldigi) redraws the letters. A soft crackle to the ear (sheet 29).

4fsk.h: Four frequency levels: each symbol carries two bits.
4fsk.l: A rectangular block 6 to 12.5 kHz wide, full like noise, often in bursts (DMR splits the channel into two time slots). A hoarse "frrr" to the ear (sheet 46).

mt63.h: 64 tones at once, each slowly modulated, with lots of redundancy.
mt63.l: A flat block of 1 or 2 kHz centred on 1500 Hz, with sharp edges; a steady hiss. Even works through a microphone held to a loudspeaker (sheet 31).

lora.h: The frequency sweeps the whole width, then starts again from the bottom: the position of the jump carries the data.
lora.l: Parallel diagonals, easy to recognise: Meshtastic and MeshCore on 869.525 MHz or 433 MHz, LoRaWAN sensors (sheets 13, 23 and 24).

sstv.h: A sync pulse at 1200 Hz, then the frequency follows the brightness of the line, from 1500 (black) to 2300 Hz (white).
sstv.l: Regular sync lines and a cloud that changes with the picture; a "chirping" sound for one to two minutes. 14.230 MHz, ISS on 145.800 MHz (sheet 37).
r: VIS header, then lines: 1200 Hz sync, green, blue, red; here 20 lines of a test pattern
QSSTV, MMSSTV, Robot36 on a smartphone

fax.t: Weather fax: 1500 Hz black, 2300 Hz white
fax.h: The frequency moves continuously from black to white, 120 lines per minute.
fax.l: Two fixed bands at 1500 and 2300 Hz (800 Hz apart), a steady "tick-tock". Published frequencies are carrier frequencies: listen in USB 1.9 kHz lower (sheet 38).
r: 300 Hz start tone, phasing lines (white pulse), then the chart

elt.h: An AM signal whose tone falls from 1600 to 300 Hz, two to four times per second.
elt.l: A fixed carrier and sidebands sliding like a fan: the "woo-woo" of distress beacons, also on 121.375 MHz for exercises (sheets 27 and 28).

406.h: Half a second of transmission: 160 ms of pure carrier, then the phase swings by ±1.1 radian at 400 bit/s.
406.l: A short little line coming back every 50 s, between 406.0 and 406.1 MHz; nothing useful to hear, a decoder is needed (EPIRB 406, sheet 28).

adsb.h: 0.5 µs pulses whose position carries the bits (PPM); here the time scale is greatly slowed down.
adsb.l: Very short horizontal lines across the whole width, hundreds per second near an airport; an SDR dongle is needed (sheet 15).

acars.h: An AM signal carrying two tones, 1200 and 2400 Hz, at 2400 bit/s.
acars.l: Half-second bursts with carrier and sidebands, on 131.525, 131.725 or 131.825 MHz in Europe: a "brrrt" to the ear (sheet 16).

ais.t: AIS: GMSK 9600 baud on two channels
ais.h: A smoothed FSK (GMSK) in 26 ms bursts, once on 161.975 MHz, once on 162.025 MHz (reduced scale).
ais.l: Two columns of short little lines, 50 kHz apart, a regular clicking; the more ships, the denser it gets (sheet 19).

navtex.t: NAVTEX and DSC on medium and short waves: 170 Hz FSK
navtex.h: Like RTTY: two frequencies 170 Hz apart, but at 100 baud.
navtex.l: Two parallel lines, continuous during the bulletin, on 518 and 490 kHz (NAVTEX) or 2187.5 kHz (digital selective calling) (sheet 20).
r: SITOR-B, CCIR 476: 7 bits with four "1"s, with FEC repetition

hfdl.h: A 1800 baud PSK on a 1440 Hz subcarrier.
hfdl.l: Bursts about 2.4 kHz wide between 2.9 and 22 MHz; a modem hiss that comes and goes (sheet 17).

ctcss.t: CTCSS: a sub-tone under the voice
ctcss.h: A low continuous tone (67 to 254 Hz, here 88.5 Hz) added to the voice.
ctcss.l: Seen in the FM receiver audio: a fixed line at the very bottom, under the voice; it opens the squelch of repeaters and walkie-talkies (sheet 10).

dtmf.h: Each keypad key sends a low tone (697 to 941 Hz) and a high one (1209 to 1633 Hz) at the same time.
dtmf.l: Pairs of dots aligned on eight fixed columns; the "beep-beep" of phone numbers and repeater commands (sheet 10).

selcall.h: Five 100 ms tones one after the other, one per digit.
selcall.l: A small staircase of dots, repeated; a quick "tululululu" to call one specific radio (sheet 33).
r: 1 2 3 4 5, twice; also decoded by the SelCall app of the UV-K1

pocsag.h: An FSK at ±4.5 kHz; a 1010… preamble then the data (reduced scale).
pocsag.l: Two clean lines during the preamble, then a full band; a shrill "brrrrt". 466.075 MHz, DAPNET 439.9875 MHz (sheet 45).

ale.t: ALE: automatic link establishment on shortwave
ale.h: Eight tones from 750 to 2500 Hz, 125 baud, in bursts.
ale.l: A block about 2 kHz wide made of small dots, one to two seconds, sometimes on several nearby frequencies; a high-pitched twitter (sheet 34).

rs41.h: A smoothed FSK at 4800 baud, non-stop; the frequency drifts slowly as the sonde rises and cools down.
rs41.l: A band about 10 kHz wide that slides at an angle during the whole flight, between 400 and 406 MHz (sheet 21).

ook.h: The carrier switches on and off in short or long pulses (on-off keying); the message is repeated three times.
ook.l: Bursts of small dots, often in threes, on 433.92 MHz: weather stations, temperature probes, remote controls (sheet 22).

fhss.h: The frequency changes 1600 times per second among 79 channels (reduced scale).
fhss.l: Small lines scattered everywhere over 80 MHz, never in the same place, around 2.4 GHz (sheet 25).

wspr.h: Four tones spaced 1.46 Hz, 0.68 s per symbol, for 110.6 s.
wspr.l: A very thin line about 6 Hz wide lasting almost two minutes, every even two minutes: you have to zoom in a lot (sheet 29).

qrss.h: A carrier switched on and off, with dots of 3 to 10 s, often on two nearby frequencies (DFCW).
qrss.l: Lines a few Hz wide, read on a ten-minute screen; inaudible to the ear (sheet 30).
qrss.n: sped up: 0.6 s dot instead of 3 to 10 s

texte.h: Each line of a picture becomes a group of tones: the sound is like noise.
texte.l: The text or drawing appears directly on the SDR screen (sheet 40).
r: Sent from the bottom of the picture: upright on the live waterfall, upside down in the footprint (read from top to bottom)

vara.t: Modern HF data: VARA, Pactor, ARDOP
vara.h: Long full bursts (OFDM or PSK) and, in between, short replies from the other station.
vara.l: A rectangle about 2.4 kHz wide that stops and starts again, with a small acknowledgement in between; a chopped hiss (sheet 29).

chirp.h: A slow frequency ramp crossing the whole HF band; echoes from the ionosphere arrive a little later.
chirp.l: A diagonal sweeping the screen, doubled by parallel lines (the echoes); a "ffweet" that passes in a fraction of a second.

oth.h: Pulses repeated 10 to 50 times per second, each several kHz wide.
oth.l: A wide striped block covering whole bands; a very regular woodpecker knocking on shortwave.

parasites.t: Interference from a switching power supply
parasites.h: A square wave: its frequency and all its harmonics come out at the same time.
parasites.l: A comb of regular lines drifting together, on a noise background: look for it with NOISE FIND or a portable receiver (sheet K22).

mpx.h: The demodulated sound (multiplex) contains the L+R channel, a 19 kHz pilot, the L-R channel around 38 kHz and RDS at 57 kHz.
mpx.l: Seen from 0 to 60 kHz after demodulation: a low block, a thin line at 19 kHz, a weaker block in the middle and RDS at the very top (sheet 12).
r: With headphones: 4 s in mono (the middle block, L-R, disappears), then 4 s in stereo, the melody on the left and the chords on the right.

dcf77.h: A carrier dropping to 15 % for 0.1 s (bit 0) or 0.2 s (bit 1), at the start of each second.
dcf77.l: A fixed line with a black gap every second; the 59th second has none, to mark the minute (sheet 12).
r: Here the carrier is brought down to 1000 Hz; the 6th second has no gap, like the 59th second of each minute

ofdm.h: Many tightly packed carriers, each slow: the sum looks like noise.
ofdm.l: A flat rectangle with sharp edges, always there: DRM on shortwave (10 kHz), DAB+ (1.5 MHz), DVB-T, Wi-Fi. A continuous hiss to the ear (sheets 12 and 25).

dsss.h: The data are mixed with a very fast code: the energy is spread over a wide band.
dsss.l: A wide hump, barely above the noise; GPS is even below the noise and cannot be seen without processing (sheets 25 and 26).

hline.h: Cold hydrogen in the Milky Way emits a very faint hiss on 1420.405 MHz. The motion of the galaxy's arms shifts it by the Doppler effect: you see several small humps.
hline.l: Almost nothing in the waterfall from one second to the next: you have to average for a long time to see the humps rise out of the noise. Here, look at the average spectrum when stopped. A dish or a horn, a preamp and an SDR dongle are enough.

sun.h: Electrons thrown out by a flare cross the Sun's corona and make it emit at lower and lower frequencies as they move away.
sun.l: Lines falling diagonally from the top to the bottom of the spectrum in less than a second, over a background of solar noise; a swelling "shhhh". From about 10 to 400 MHz, also on shortwave around 20 MHz.

jupiter.h: Jupiter's magnetic field and its moon Io produce powerful emissions between 15 and 40 MHz: slow L bursts and very short S bursts that slide down fast.
jupiter.l: First waves of hiss (L, like surf on a beach), then trains of little "pops" (S) in tight diagonals. Around 20.1 MHz at night, with a simple dipole, when Io is well placed.

pulsar.h: A spinning neutron star sweeps the Earth with a radio beam, here every 0.714 s. Interstellar gas delays the low frequencies: each pulse arrives first at the top of the spectrum.
pulsar.l: A regular "tick"; in the waterfall each pulse is a curve sloping down (dispersion). The real signal is below the noise: you need a big antenna and must add up the pulses over their period.

meteor.t: Meteor echoes from the GRAVES radar (143.050 MHz)
meteor.h: The French GRAVES radar transmits non-stop on 143.050 MHz. When a shooting star ionises the air, its trail reflects a little of that signal to your receiver, for a fraction of a second to a few seconds.
meteor.l: In USB on 143.049 MHz: short "pings" around 1000 Hz, sometimes an echo that slides (the meteor head, Doppler effect) or one that lasts. Far more during showers (Perseids, Geminids) (sheet 1).

whistler.h: Lightning makes a radio click; part of it follows the Earth's magnetic field lines to the other hemisphere and back, high notes first.
whistler.l: A "pyooo" falling from high to low in one or two seconds, right after a click; crackles (sferics) everywhere. Below 10 kHz, with a VLF receiver far from power lines.

chorus.h: During a magnetic storm, electrons trapped in the magnetosphere emit small rising notes, mostly around sunrise.
chorus.l: Overlapping rising chirps, like birds, from about 1 to 4 kHz. Same equipment as for whistlers.

sputnik.h: The first artificial satellite sent beeps of about 0.3 s on 20.005 and 40.002 MHz, alternately, for three weeks.
sputnik.l: A regularly broken line: "beep… beep…", the sound the whole world listened to in October 1957 (reconstruction).

doppler.h: A low-orbit satellite comes closer then moves away: the received frequency falls during the pass, by about ±3 kHz at 145 MHz and ±10 kHz at 435 MHz.
doppler.l: A line falling in an S shape: slowly at first, fast when the satellite is closest, then slowly again (sheet 41).

apt.h: A 2400 Hz subcarrier amplitude-modulated by the picture, two lines per second, with a sync pulse at the start of each line. Stopped in 2025; Meteor-M satellites now transmit LRPT.
apt.l: A line at 2400 Hz with sidebands that change with the picture, and the famous "tick-tock" twice a second (sheet 41).

eme.h: A signal sent to the Moon comes back about 2.5 s later, hugely weakened, slightly smeared and shifted by Doppler.
eme.l: You hear your own "beep", then its faint, slightly blurred echo 2.5 s later. Radio amateurs do it in CW or JT65, on 144 MHz and above (sheet 1).

msk144.h: Two tones, 1000 and 2000 Hz, at 2000 baud, in 72 ms frames repeated non-stop: each meteor trail lets a few of them through.
msk144.l: Bursts of 0.1 to 1 s, about 2.4 kHz wide, that appear and fade with the meteor's "ping". On 50 and 144 MHz, with WSJT-X.

jt65.h: One sync tone and 64 data tones spaced 2.7 Hz (JT65A), 0.37 s per symbol, 47 s of transmission per minute.
jt65.l: A ladder of small lines over about 180 Hz, with a sync line that keeps returning to the same place. Used for Moon bounce (JT65B and C) and very weak signals.

tetra.h: π/4-DQPSK phase modulation at 18,000 symbols per second, four time-shared channels, in 25 kHz channels.
tetra.l: A full block with rounded edges, always there near a base station; a hoarse hiss. Encrypted: you cannot listen to it (sheet 46).

ndb.h: A fixed carrier on long wave, with a two- or three-letter Morse identifier sent on a tone (often 1020 Hz).
ndb.l: A fixed line in the centre and, during the identifier, two small lines on either side. Roughly 190 to 535 kHz, in SSB or CW (sheet 12).

vor.h: In AM: a 30 Hz signal that depends on direction, a 9960 Hz subcarrier frequency-modulated at 30 Hz (the reference), and the Morse identifier on 1020 Hz.
vor.l: In the demodulated sound: a low 30 Hz hum, a wide wavy line near 10 kHz, and the identifier now and then (sheet 18).

ils.h: In AM, two tones of 90 and 150 Hz; their ratio tells the aircraft whether it is left or right of the centreline. The Morse identifier starts with I.
ils.l: In the demodulated sound: two very low lines at 90 and 150 Hz, and the identifier on 1020 Hz. Between 108.1 and 112 MHz; the glide slope is around 330 MHz (sheet 18).

m10.h: One frame per second, in fast FSK (about 9600 baud): wider than the RS41. Launched in France by Météo-France.
m10.l: A wide burst every second that drifts slowly during the flight; between 400 and 406 MHz (sheet 21).

tpms.h: Each wheel now and then sends an FSK burst of a few milliseconds: pressure, temperature, identifier.
tpms.l: Small isolated bursts on 433.92 MHz (or 315 MHz), often in pairs, as a car passes. Decoded by rtl_433.

als162.h: The carrier of France Inter's former long-wave service; the time is coded by small, inaudible phase modulations.
als162.l: A fixed line, very strong in France, barely widened at the start of each second; a decoder is needed to read the time (sheet 12).

wwv.h: In AM: a 5 ms "tick" at 1000 Hz every second, a 500 or 600 Hz tone, a time code on 100 Hz and a voice announcing UTC.
wwv.l: In the demodulated sound: a 500 Hz line broken every second, the 1000 Hz tick, and the code at the very bottom on 100 Hz (sheet 12).

msf.h: The carrier is switched off at the start of each second for 0.1, 0.2 or 0.3 s depending on the bits, and for 0.5 s to mark the minute.
msf.l: A fixed line with complete black gaps every second, longer than with DCF77 (sheet 12).

type2.h: The shock wave of a coronal mass ejection makes the plasma emit lower and lower, slowly, often in two bands (the fundamental and its double).
type2.l: Two parallel noise bands drifting down gently for several minutes. Compare with type III bursts, which are much faster.

tweeks.h: At night, the click of distant lightning bounces between the ground and the ionosphere; frequencies near the cut-off (around 1.7 kHz) arrive last.
tweeks.l: A small "ping" that falls and stops around 1.7 kHz, sometimes with an echo at double frequency; crackles everywhere. Below 10 kHz, at night.

hiss.h: Wideband noise produced by electrons in the plasmasphere, rising and falling with magnetic activity.
hiss.l: A band of hiss from a few hundred Hz to a few kHz, with no pattern, slowly swelling and fading.

aurora.h: The aurora reflects VHF waves but shakes them very fast: each signal is spread over several hundred Hz.
aurora.l: CW turns into a raspy hiss, as if whispered; you no longer hear a note. On 50 and 144 MHz, beaming north during magnetic storms.

galactic.h: The centre of the galaxy emits a radio hiss that Karl Jansky discovered in 1932 around 20 MHz. It rises and falls as the Earth turns.
galactic.l: A background noise that slowly rises then falls again, about 4 minutes earlier each day. Visible with a simple dipole between 20 and 40 MHz.

cubesat.h: Small satellites regularly send their measurements (battery, temperatures) in FSK or GMSK at 1200 or 9600 baud, around 435–438 MHz.
cubesat.l: Regular bursts sliding lower each time, by the Doppler effect, during the pass (sheet 41).

issfm.h: Astronauts talk with schools and radio amateurs in FM on 145.800 MHz. The station flies at 28,000 km/h: during the pass, the received frequency slides from about +3.5 kHz to −3.5 kHz.
issfm.l: A band of FM voice slowly moving from right to left during the 10-minute pass (sheet 41).

buzzer.h: A Russian military station that has sent, for decades, a buzz of about one second repeated about 25 times a minute, sometimes interrupted by a voice message.
buzzer.l: A fixed carrier and, at each buzz, a column of tight lines from top to bottom. Easy to find on 4625 kHz in USB.

pip.h: Another Russian military shortwave beacon, repeating short little beeps day and night, sometimes interrupted by messages.
pip.l: A fixed line cut by a short beep about 50 times a minute; to the ear, a steady "pip… pip…" that never stops.

squeaky.h: A Russian military shortwave beacon, named by listeners after its repeated sound pattern.
squeaky.l: A small pattern of two sounds, one of them rising, repeated in a loop: like a squeaking wheel.

codar.h: Coastal radars sweep a band of frequencies once or twice a second to measure currents and waves.
codar.l: Regular parallel diagonals and a repeated "swish"; around 4.5–5.5 MHz, 13 MHz and 25 MHz, often day and night.

stanag.h: 8-PSK phase modulation at 2400 baud on an 1800 Hz carrier, with a probe sequence every 107 ms to track the channel.
stanag.l: A full block about 3 kHz wide; to the ear, a hiss with a regular buzz (sheet 43).

link11.h: Sixteen tones from 605 to 2915 Hz sent together, each phase-modulated 75 times per second.
link11.l: A comb of fourteen regular lines from 935 to 2365 Hz, plus two lines set apart at 605 and 2915 Hz; to the ear, a musical drone (sheet 43).

numbers.h: At a fixed time, a short call melody, then a voice (often synthetic) reads groups of five digits, in AM or SSB.
numbers.l: The melody as separate notes, then regular groups of syllables separated by silences (sheet 43).

rttydwd.h: Like amateur RTTY, but at 50 baud with a 450 Hz shift: the German weather service sends its bulletins and marine forecasts in plain text.
rttydwd.l: Two lines much further apart, and a slightly faster rhythm. Between bulletins, the call "CQ CQ CQ DE DDK2 DDH7 DDK9" then RYRYRY. On 4583, 7646 and 10,100.8 kHz, also 147.3 kHz (sheet 32).

mfsk16.h: Sixteen tones spaced 15.625 Hz, one at a time, 15.625 times per second; each tone carries four bits, protected by error correction.
mfsk16.l: A 316 Hz band made of small steps that keep jumping, after a steady tone at the start. To the ear, a quick little tune, like a flute. Also used to send small pictures.

sitora.h: The station sends blocks of three characters (210 ms, 100 baud, 170 Hz shift) every 450 ms; between blocks, the other station answers with a short signal meaning "received" or "repeat".
sitora.l: Short regular bursts with a small, weaker reply in between: a cricket-like "chirp-chirp". Now rare on shortwave.

dscvhf.t: DSC: digital selective calling on channel 70
dscvhf.h: A burst of about half a second at 1200 baud, on two tones of 1300 and 2100 Hz: it carries the ship's MMSI number, the type of call and, in distress, its position.
dscvhf.l: A short, high-pitched "brrrt" on 156.525 MHz that starts with a run of alternating bits. On medium and short waves, DSC is 100 baud FSK, like NAVTEX (sheet 20).

selcal.t: SELCAL: selective calling of aircraft on shortwave
selcal.h: Air traffic control calls one particular aircraft with two pulses of about one second, each made of two tones out of sixteen (312.6 to 1479.1 Hz). In the aircraft a light and a chime go off: the crew does not have to listen all the time.
selcal.l: Two successive chords, "bing-bong", between the voice messages on aeronautical SSB frequencies, for example 5616 or 8864 kHz.

dcs.h: Instead of a continuous tone like CTCSS, the radio sends under the voice a 23-bit word repeated non-stop at 134.4 bits per second. At the end, a 134.4 Hz tone closes the squelch silently.
dcs.l: Seen in the FM receiver audio: an irregular band at the very bottom, below 300 Hz, and a dull rumble if the radio's filter lets it through (sheet 10).

t1750.h: A short 1750 Hz tone (about 0.5 to 1 s) at the start of a transmission still opens some European amateur repeaters; the repeater often answers with a beep when you release.
t1750.l: A short line at 1750 Hz, then the voice, then the repeater's beep (sheet 10).

ncdxf.h: Eighteen beacons around the world transmit in turn, ten seconds each, on 14.100, 18.110, 21.150, 24.930 and 28.200 MHz: the call sign in Morse, then four one-second dashes at 100 W, 10 W, 1 W and 0.1 W.
ncdxf.l: A call sign, then four dashes getting weaker and weaker: if you can still hear the last one, propagation to that beacon is excellent. Here 4U1UN (New York) then VE8AT (Canada) (sheet 30).

lrpt.h: The Russian Meteor-M weather satellites send their images digitally: four-state phase modulation (QPSK), 72,000 symbols per second, about 120 kHz wide.
lrpt.l: A full block with rounded edges that slides slowly during the pass (Doppler effect); to the ear, just a hiss. On 137.9 or 137.1 MHz, decoded with SatDump (sheet 41).

quindar.h: When Houston presses the microphone key, a 2525 Hz beep (250 ms) switches on the ground station transmitters; on release, a 2475 Hz beep switches them off.
quindar.l: A high beep before each sentence and another, slightly lower, after it: the famous sound of the Apollo mission recordings.

wow.h: The Big Ear radio telescope (Ohio) picked up, for 72 seconds, a narrow and very strong signal near the hydrogen line, around 1420.456 MHz. Astronomer Jerry Ehman wrote "Wow!" on the printout. It was never seen again and its origin is still debated.
wow.l: A thin line that rises out of the noise, grows and fades: the shape of a fixed source drifting through the antenna beam. This is a reconstruction: no sound recording exists.

frb.h: A radio flash lasting a few milliseconds, coming from another galaxy; the first one was discovered in 2007. The gas it crosses delays the low frequencies a lot: the burst arrives smeared, high notes first.
frb.l: A single curve falling from the top to the bottom of the spectrum, then nothing. Some repeat; most are seen only once.

letterb.h: Russian navy transmitters endlessly repeat a single Morse letter, each 100 Hz from its neighbour: D, P, S, C, A, F, K or M depending on the site.
letterb.l: Parallel dotted lines, very close together, each with its own rhythm. Around 4558, 5154, 7039, 10,872, 13,528 and 16,332 kHz, in CW.

sid.h: Navy VLF transmitters (20.9 kHz in France, 23.4 kHz in Germany…) travel between the ground and the ionosphere. When a solar flare arrives, its X-rays change the bottom of the ionosphere within minutes and the received level jumps.
sid.l: A narrow, steady band (the transmitter's MSK signal) that suddenly gets stronger, then slowly returns to normal. A wire loop and a sound card are enough: a classic astronomy-club project.

qrn.h: Every lightning stroke is a very powerful transmitter covering all frequencies at once. On medium and short waves you can hear storms thousands of kilometres away, mostly in summer and on the low bands.
qrn.l: Irregular horizontal lines across the whole width; sharp crashes to the ear. The noise blanker (NB) helps a little, a loop antenna helps more.

fading.h: On shortwave the signal arrives by several paths through the ionosphere. Depending on the frequency they add up or cancel out: a narrow dip wanders through the signal.
fading.l: A dark zone drifting slowly through the AM station. When it crosses the carrier, in the centre, the sound turns harsh and distorted for a few seconds; synchronous detection or listening in SSB cures it.

plc.t: PLC: Internet through the mains sockets
plc.h: Powerline adapters send data over the house wiring on hundreds of carriers between 2 and 30 MHz (higher for recent models), one every 24.4 kHz. The wires radiate like an antenna.
plc.l: A comb of regular lines flickering in packets, with gaps on the amateur bands (notches required by the standard); to the ear, a crackle that follows the Internet traffic (sheet 43).

fence.h: The energiser sends a pulse of several thousand volts into the wire about once a second. If grass touches the wire or an insulator is damaged, a spark jumps and radiates on all frequencies.
fence.l: A very thin horizontal line across the whole width, at a perfectly regular interval; a "tick… tick…" from long wave up to VHF. Its steady rhythm tells it apart from storm static.

gsm.t: GSM phone next to a loudspeaker
gsm.h: A 2G phone transmits in bursts of 0.577 ms, 217 times per second. A poorly shielded audio amplifier detects these bursts and makes them audible.
gsm.l: A comb of lines every 217 Hz; the famous "dit-dit-di-di-dit" just before the phone rings, then a steady buzz during the call. Getting rare: 2G networks are being switched off.

jjy.h: Each second the carrier is at full power for 0.8 s (bit 0), 0.5 s (bit 1) or 0.2 s (marker), then drops to 10 %. It is the reverse of DCF77, which drops at the start of the second.
jjy.l: A fixed line that weakens at the end of each second, sooner or later. Transmitters in Fukushima (40 kHz) and Saga-Fukuoka (60 kHz), for Japan's radio-controlled clocks.

rwm.h: In telegraphy on 4996, 9996 and 14,996 kHz: one 100 ms pulse every second, then, at other minutes, ten pulses per second. The call sign RWM is sent in Morse twice an hour.
rwm.l: The call sign, then a line cut into regular "ticks", then into fast dots. Listen in CW or SSB.

bpm.h: The Pucheng station (Shaanxi) transmits in AM on 2.5, 5, 10 and 15 MHz: a 10 ms tick at 1000 Hz every second (300 ms on the minute) and, at certain minutes, 100 ms ticks for UT1 time. The call sign BPM is given in Morse, then by a voice.
bpm.l: In the demodulated sound: the call sign, then very short lines at 1000 Hz, one per second, with a longer one on the minute. Often mixed with WWV on the same frequencies.
